newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia electoral referendum ends on low turnout.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia electoral referendum ends on low turnout.

text.p: Voting in a Slovenian referendum on changing the electoral system ended on Sunday and official figures showed less than a third of the electorate bothered to take part.

About 1.5 million people were eligible to choose one of three possible models for a new electoral system. The referendum follows an inconclusive general election a month ago that gave neither right or left a mandate to govern.
Official figures showed turnout at 30.16 percent, compared with 73.7 percent at the end of the general election on November 10.
A commentator on Slovenian state television blamed the low turnout on a failure to explain clearly to voters the differences between the election systems proposed.

Television said the referendum cost the country 400 million tolars ($2.8 million) just a month after 450 million tolars were spent on Slovenia's second general election since independence from Yugoslavia in 1991.
The first unofficial results were expected later on Sunday and the final official result will be announced on Thursday.
President Milan Kucan, Slovenia's former communist party chief who is still hugely popular for his role in the country's independence drive, remained non-partisan in commenting on the referendum.
"The best electoral system is the one that most people choose," he told national radio.
But if one electoral system fails to win 50 percent support, the referendum will be deemed null and void.

Recent opinion polls have suggested a two-round majority system proposed by the centre-right Social Democrats was likely to get the most backing. Under this model, a candidate would need to secure an absolute majority in two rounds of voting to win each of Slovenia's 88 voting districts.
Such a system was more likely to favour the bigger parties and produce a better chance of a clear result in a general election.
The centre-left Liberal Democrats (LDS), Slovenia's strongest party, favour proportional representation in which each party would put up a list of 88 candidates.

The National Council (lower house of parliament) proposes a model combining Social Democrat and LDS models, with half of the 88 candidates elected on the basis of a two-round run-off system and the rest by proportional representation.

An alliance of right-wing parties failed to win an absolute majority in the November election by just one seat. Talks between Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek's Liberal Democrats, the alliance and smaller parties have gone on for the past month to try and form a new coalition government.
